samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B states what the call has to achieve and the dated next step up front. Its questions are open, specific to refrigeration and listed in order, and it explicitly says to get the failure-cost figure from her rather than suggesting one. A is solid but looser: some of its questions can be answered yes or no, its objection handling has the seller bring their own cost math, it doesn't say when to ask about the decision process, and its next step has no date. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A sets a clear goal for the call and a gate check: a dated second meeting with the person who approves spend. It gets the cost of a failure from her, explicitly without suggesting a number. Every unknown is something to find out, and nothing is assumed. B is solid general sales prep, but several questions can be answered yes or no, decision process gets one line with no timing, its next step has no date, and its objection math starts from the seller's numbers.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A sets a clear goal for the call with a gate check, keeps facts it knows apart from ones still to learn, and says to get the cost of a failure from her without suggesting a number. B is solid, but several of its questions can be answered yes or no, and it states 'thousands in product' itself instead of drawing the number out of her. B also never says when in the call to ask about who decides. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B states a clear goal for the call and ends with a dated next step that has an owner. It also asks open questions about refrigeration specifically, says outright to get the cost figure from her rather than suggest one, and keeps what's known separate from what's still to learn. A is well organized but vaguer. Several of its questions can be answered yes or no, and it states 'thousands in product' as fact and suggests proof-point numbers instead of having her supply the cost. Its close also lacks a specific date.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B sets a clear outcome for the call and checks for it with gate criteria. Its questions are open-ended and specific to refrigeration, and it tells the seller to get the cost of a failure from her rather than suggest one. It ends with a dated next step that names who should attend. A is solid and practical, but its goal is softer, several of its questions can be answered yes or no, and it never explicitly says to let her put the number on failure cost. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A says exactly what has to be true by the end of the call: a problem she can put a size on, a signer or a way to reach one, and something she'll commit to. It also tells you to get the failure cost from her, never suggest a number, and end on a dated call with the decision-maker. B has good ramen-specific detail (stocks, tare, a central prep kitchen) and good objection handling, but its goal is looser, several questions can be answered yes or no, and it leans on the seller framing the cost (one emergency call plus lost inventory) instead of drawing the number out of her.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A is clearer that the call never gave the buyer a reason to act. Its questions about problem, signer and date show what should have been settled before sending material, and it gives a message with one narrow question, a dated step and an easy way out. Answer B hedges ('almost certainly not a no'), barely covers what should have happened on the call, and recommends a longer multi-touch chase before stopping. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B explains more clearly that 'send me info' wasn't progress and that he never named a problem, a signer or a date. That also covers what should have been settled before sending anything, which A barely addresses. Both give good follow-up messages, but B's question is easy to answer and offers a clear way out, and B also says when to stop and how to rank the deal in the pipeline.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B explains why the deck gave him no reason to act, and its draft asks one clear question with a specific time slot and easy exits. Its follow-up sequence is tighter, and it says outright to mark the deal low in the forecast. A states the polite-brush-off point more directly, but its draft makes two asks, its chase cadence is longer and leans on breakup-email tactics, and it barely says what should have been agreed before sending the material. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B's main advantage is that it says plainly that 'send me info' was likely a polite way to end the call, which is the central diagnosis; A only implies this through the missing next step. Both include strong drafts that avoid 'just checking in'. B has a clearer dated follow-up sequence with a breakup email and a point to stop. A is a little better at avoiding pressure and at advising a dated follow-up on the next call, but neither clearly says what should have been asked before agreeing to send the material.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain the soft brush-off well and give a usable email, but B covers all three discovery steps the seller skipped: what the material was meant to help him decide, who else is involved, and a booked follow-up. B's message makes one specific ask and offers a clear way out. A's email bundles several asks, and its suggestion to use a 'regulatory deadline' as a hook leans toward false urgency, while B explicitly rules out urgency and gives a cleaner point at which to stop chasing. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain that 'send me information' is a polite way to end a call, and both give a usable recovery email. A is better on the specifics. Its 'next time' advice covers all three things that should have happened before sending material, its email makes one easy request with a clear way out, and it rules out false urgency outright. B's email bundles several requests, and B suggests mentioning a regulatory deadline, which comes close to manufactured urgency. B also suggests contacting other stakeholders around him.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers take the same clear position: offer scoped trials and do the setup for the clinic. A does more to tell a prospect gathering options from one with a real problem, using a sizeable problem, a named signer and what the clinic will commit, and it sets a fuller success test with dates and pricing. B adds a useful option to pilot one team or a paid pilot, but its qualifying step is thin. Neither gives ready wording for answering a prospect, though A comes closer with its call questions and its line for the cofounder. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers take a clear position and deal with the setup day by offering to load the schedule for the clinic. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers see that the day of setup is the real cost and offer to do the setup for the prospect. Both also recommend agreed success criteria and screening prospects before starting a trial. A wins mainly because it gives a ready-to-send reply for prospects who ask to try it free, which B doesn't. A also states its position more cleanly, while B both says 'don't say yes to everyone' and 'say yes to all of them'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers take a clear conditional position and see that setup is the real cost, so both offer to load the schedule for the prospect. B does more on the other items. It sets a written success test with named owners on each side and an end date, and it qualifies prospects by asking about their pain and who signs. It also gives wording to send the prospect, which A does not.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A reasons more tightly from the facts given. It lists exactly what is unknown (who signs, budget, the cost in numbers, whether finance or the owner was involved), labels every cause as a guess, and gives one diagnostic message plus a clear point to stop: close it out if she goes quiet again. B is solid and puts a number on the odds (15–25%), but it spreads across many tactics, leaves the stopping point vague, and states the Q4 peak season as if it were known. Neither answer gives a lesson to apply at the start of the next deal. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B reads the stall from the facts more clearly. It sets out what is known and unknown, and it names finance, the owner and the drivers as missing parties. It suggests one message that asks something real, offers a way out, and says what each reply would mean, including when to close the deal out. A is solid and gives a useful probability, but it spreads into several moves at once and gives a weaker point at which to stop. Neither answer gives a real lesson for the start of the next deal.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B centers on one well-worded message that gives Priya a smaller pilot step and an easy way to say no. It also sets a clear point to stop, and its lesson for next time is concrete: get a sized cost, a named signer and a buyer commitment before sending the quote. A diagnoses the stall just as well but spreads its advice across six moves and turns the lesson into questions rather than a practice. B's opening claim that the deal did not lose on price or to a competitor is stated more firmly than the facts support, and it lists price as a possible cause later anyway. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers read the silence well and point out the missing signer, deadline and business case. A's next step is more useful: one complete message with a pilot offer, a choice to close the deal out, and a specific call time, followed by a clear rule for when to stop. B lists six separate moves, and its one-pager depends on numbers the seller doesn't have, though B is a bit more direct about how unlikely the deal is to close and names the owner/CFO gap more clearly.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A reads the silence from the facts given (no date, no owner, unknown signer), labels its causes as guesses, and gives one low-pressure message with full wording that asks for the approval path and a dated step. Answer B is more candid about the odds and touches on a lesson for future deals. However, it offers a scattered list of moves, and its value email depends on figures the user hasn't got. Neither answer says much about what to do differently at the start of the next deal. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B reads the silence more closely from the facts given: no date, no owner, no known signer. It also gives one low-pressure message with full wording that asks what Q1 depends on and who else is involved. A covers similar causes but offers seven scattered moves, adds cost-of-waiting pressure and is vaguer about when to stop. Neither answer clearly names a lesson for the start of the next deal, though A at least points to the missing decision-maker, date and cost as gaps to close next time.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B names the notes' specific strengths, makes one concrete change and two small fill-ins, and clearly says to send them. A gives a short compliment and then lists many fixes and gaps, some of them invented: it claims the 'margin' point is wrong, adds a computed $95k figure, says the 14 cold quotes read as fact, and asks for more process. Its date check is a fair catch, but it brings in context the request didn't give. B's one small slip is saying the $6,800 is labeled as Marcus's estimate, which is only partly true. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A says plainly that the notes are strong and names their real strengths: his own numbers, the decision path, the dated next step and the risk plan. It then makes one well-argued change and two minor fill-ins, and its suggested wording stays close to the original. Answer B piles on fixes and gaps, invents a $95k headline figure, and asks for extra items like competitors, accountant veto power and a day-7 check-in. Its date objection is also shaky, since the prompt says today is 4 Nov 2026, not the 28 Oct date B gives.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers praise the notes but then list many gaps, which goes against the rubric's call for only a few small edits. A stays closer to the original facts, warns against adding a dollar total, and ends with a clear call: fix these points, then send. B adds new numbers (a $95k/month figure and an 'under 1 day' target), gets today's date wrong (it says 28 Oct 2026; it is 4 Nov 2026), asks for an extra summary section, and never clearly says whether to send. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers treat already-strong notes as needing heavy revision and pile on gaps, sections and process, so both do poorly on rubric items 2, 3 and 5. B's praise is more specific, and it avoids adding new figures, even warning against a dollar total. A computes a $95k/month figure, proposes an 'under 1 day' metric that isn't in the notes, and misstates today's date (28 Oct instead of 4 Nov 2026). B also gives a conditional judgment ('fix the four gaps before sending'), while A gives no send-or-hold judgment at all.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A names exactly what the notes do well: Marcus's own numbers, a signer who can approve $9k alone, owners on both sides and a dated next step. It then proposes one small change (move the success-criteria question before the proposal) plus two light checks, without restructuring anything. Answer B also praises the notes, but it lists eight or more fixes and asks for new sections such as competing vendors, the invoicing system and a timeline worked back from 1 March. It adds details that aren't in the notes (turnaround under 1 day, 56 quotes a month), gets today's date wrong, and its verdict is 'fix before sending' rather than send. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B names what the notes do well (Marcus's own numbers, the decision path, the dated next step with owners, the stall plan) and suggests one main change with replacement text that stays close to the original wording. A treats strong notes as flawed: it lists four 'fix before sending' items and several smaller gaps, asks for extra context, timeline work and a mid-pilot check-in, and also gets today's date wrong. B never says outright to send the notes, but 'Your notes already work' and its short list of checks make its verdict much clearer than A's.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn down the 40% discount, explain the poor fit, and give honest wording that keeps the door open without pressure. B is slightly stronger: it names more consequences (churn in 3 to 6 months, a bad impression with other makers, a low reference price) and gives a ready-to-use script for the manager conversation. A's branching plan for the call is useful, but its quota advice is thinner, and neither answer works out the price as a share of her revenue or suggests where else to spend selling time. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recognize that the problem is fit, not just price, and both warn that she is likely to churn. A takes a firmer stand against the 40% discount and gives the user a ready script for the manager. B's 'don't lead with 40%' is softer, and its scheduled yes-or-no decision call adds a little push to close, though B does add a useful referral ask and branching follow-ups.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers advise against the 40% discount and point to fit as the real problem. A weakens its own advice by suggesting discounts tied to milestones and, at the end, a fallback 10-20% concession. B stays consistent: it starts with a question about her actual pain, offers a right-sized plan at its normal price or none at all, and reopens the conversation when she hits a trigger number she picks herself. B also handles the manager more clearly. B's push to book a dated follow-up during the call is a little sales-driven, but it is not pressure. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say no to the 40% discount and explain that the real problem is fit, not price. A holds that position all the way through: it offers a smaller plan only at its normal price, lets her set the point at which to come back, and gives a clear plan for the manager and for prospecting. B weakens its own advice by suggesting tied discounts and a 10-20% time-limited concession, and it picks the 5+ account trigger for her.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers advise against the 40% discount, see that the real problem is fit, predict churn, and give honest wording that leaves the door open. B handles the quota pressure better: it tells the rep to spend their time on prospects with 10+ accounts and gives a clear script for the manager, and it adds the point that a deep discount resets what she expects to pay at renewal. A ends by pushing for a yes-or-no decision at a set time, which is slightly more pressure than the situation calls for. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers advise against the 40% discount, see that the problem is fit (2 wholesale accounts against a platform built for 10+), and give honest wording that leaves room to come back later. B's wording is more thorough, but its 'stop talking' tactic and the push toward a dated yes-or-no call add some closing pressure. A deals with the quota more practically by suggesting the rep spend the time on better-fit prospects, while B only suggests asking the manager for a smaller plan and the discount floor.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A is a usable page laid out in call order, with minute marks on every section. Its prompts are short enough to glance at, and its Problem section asks for the number behind each answer. Its gate check and close set a dated next step and name the signer. Answer B has stronger construction detail (WIP, lien waivers, workers' comp audits, an objections table), but it runs well past one page, puts minute marks only in a summary table, and relies on read-aloud scripts, which works against the request for something to glance at mid-call. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B follows the call in order, with a minute mark on every section. It is more compact, and it focuses on sizing the problem in the prospect's own numbers, ending with a booked date, a time and who will attend. A is very specific to subcontractors, but it runs long and is not in conversation order: it adds pain-signal, objection and after-call sections and quotes full scripts to read aloud, so it is harder to glance at mid-call.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both are usable, time-stamped sheets with a dated close and a fallback for losing the thread. A does better at sizing the problem in the prospect's own numbers, with its 'number you want' column and its gate check. B is more specific to subcontractors (pay apps, retainage, bonding, workers' comp audits, a spouse doing the books) and adds an objection table and a notes block for the decision maker and next-step date, so it narrowly wins as a sheet to keep beside you on the call. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a usable, time-stamped sheet that ends on a dated next step and covers subcontractor issues like job costing, retainage and bonding. B does better on finding the cost: its 'Number you want' column, its 'last time it was wrong, what did it cost' question and its gate check push the prospect to size the problem in their own numbers. A only asks 'what does that cost you' once, inside a list of pain topics. A has a cleaner notes block, but B's who-signs blanks and its 'Can [signer] join?' prompt cover the same need, and B adds a few lines of pre-call advice that slightly dilute the glance-only format.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A puts a minute mark on every section and lists each question next to the number it should get, so the cost question is built in: hours, days to close, money stuck in retainage, and what a mistake cost them. Its close names who, what and when and includes the signer. Answer B is more specific to subcontractors and includes the owner doing the books at night. However, its minute marks appear only in the opening timeline table. It also adds extra sections like objections and pain signals, which make it longer and harder to scan, and it handles who else is involved under qualifying rather than in the close. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a usable sheet specific to subcontractors. B puts minute marks on every section heading, so a nervous caller can find their place. It also ties each question to a number in the prospect's own terms, such as hours, days to close, money stuck in retainage, or what a mistake cost them. A uses a timeline table, but the sections below it have no minute marks, its cost questions are softer, and 'who else is involved' sits under Qualify instead of in the close.

A packs in sales moves the customer didn't ask for: asking for a testimonial, case study or referral, a feature showcase, a training offer, and tips about upselling seats or tiers. It also names example features the vendor may not have. Neither answer sets a specific follow-up date, and B's 'early customers' line assumes something about the customer that the request doesn't say.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A is tighter and more proportionate to a relaxed 20-minute call. It puts the customer's business changes at the centre, limits product talk to one relevant feature, and explicitly says not to upsell. B handles the renewal more cleanly, keeps the referral ask away from it, and asks for follow-up dates. However, B adds more question-heavy sections, a feature showcase, an 'expansion later' framing, and example specifics like 'one of our earliest customers' and named features that may not be true. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is tighter, fits the 20 minutes better, gives the most time to what is changing in their business, and says plainly not to upsell. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A keeps the call light and focused on listening, handles the renewal plainly, and says outright not to upsell, though its close has no date for follow-up. B adds asks for referrals, testimonials or reviews, plus heavier prep such as usage data and ticket history, which makes it feel more transactional. B also names features like route planning that the app may not have. Neither answer sets a date for the follow-up. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is a lighter, listening-focused agenda that handles the renewal plainly, rules out an upsell and suggests a recap email, though neither answer sets a follow-up date. A adds referral, testimonial and review asks, plus usage-data detective work, which makes it feel more transactional than the 'keep it light' brief. A also names specific features such as route planning that may not exist in this app.
